name: AI in Education
blurb: Artificial intelligence is already in schools, in the tools teachers plan with, the software students practise on, and the systems that run buses and budgets. These pages, built on the book The AI Ready School, set out what works from preschool to graduation, what the evidence shows, and the rule that runs through all of it: AI may inform a decision about a child, but a named person makes it.

children.name: Getting Oriented
children.blurb: The first four chapters lay the foundation for everything that follows. They explain what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool.

children.name: The Classroom
children.blurb: Part II, The Classroom, covers AI in each stage and subject. It begins with preschool through second grade, then turns to reading and writing, mathematics, science and computing, social studies and world languages, the arts and physical education, and personalized learning and tutoring.

children.name: Every Student, Every Family
children.blurb: Part III, Every Student, Every Family, covers special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. These chapters address the students and families who most need careful attention.

children.name: Running the School
children.blurb: Part IV, Running the School, covers teacher planning and grading, assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership. These chapters speak most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members.

sections.body: This part of school life is the whole of a school's use of AI, not just its operations but its effect on how children learn and its duty to protect them while that happens. The book describes AI in schools as something that can help students learn or keep them from learning, with the outcome resting on choices adults make about design, permission and supervision. It gathers 300 practical ideas across 20 chapters, from preschool through graduation and from the classroom to the business office, each carrying an evidence label of Strong, Moderate, Emerging or Practice. The labels are honest about how young the field is and tell readers how much weight each idea can bear. The reader is a teacher, a principal or district leader, a school board member, or a parent, and the Volume is written to be used rather than admired.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that the same tool produced opposite results in two trials, and the difference was how adults designed and supervised its use. It holds that people make every decision that affects a student, because when a machine decides first people rarely correct it, and that student names and details stay out of any tool without a signed data privacy agreement. Tools that help students learn give hints rather than answers, every AI draft is checked by a person before it is used, and every flag a system raises leads to a person who reaches out. What does not work is treated just as directly: AI detectors misclassify writing by students still learning English so a detection score is never proof, no evidence shows online monitoring prevents harm, and no independent evaluation of AI security systems in schools was found. The rule it holds to is that AI adoption fails when leaders mandate tools they do not use, reward logins instead of results and skip the rules, and succeeds when leaders model use, measure hours saved and student outcomes, and publish the rules for privacy, review and accountability.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from orientation to the classroom, then to families, then to running the school. Getting Oriented sets up the argument and the rules, so a leader or board member goes there first for the evidence labels, the five rules and the honest account of what is not yet known. The Classroom carries the teaching ideas for planning, feedback and grading, organized by subject and grade, which is where a teacher goes for Monday morning. Every Student, Every Family speaks to parents and to the relationship side of the work, including the finding that weekly messages about missed work, grades and absences cut course failures and that personal reminders from a student's own counselor helped students reach college while national campaigns did nothing. Running the School covers policy, pilots, purchasing and professional learning, and it is where a principal or district leader goes for the questions a board should ask, the evidence needed to answer them, the failure pattern that trips districts up, and the Thirty Day Move any school can take without buying anything.
